turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Right, Mr Brennan, before you go in I've your blood pressure at 138 over 86, your pulse is 76, temperature 36.7, and the oxygen sat is 98 percent. The doctor's ready whenever you are.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, thanks. Is 138 high, though? I had a large coffee from the garage on the way, and I was rushing because the parking on this street is a pure nightmare, so it might be up from that.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come on in and take a seat. I'm Dr O'Sullivan. What has you in today?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the head, doctor. I've had migraines for years, fifteen years easy, since I was in my early thirties and I'm forty-seven now, but this lately is different. The last while they're there when I wake, fierce, and I've been getting sick with them.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): When you say getting sick, do you mean vomiting, or the nausea beforehand?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, actually bringing stuff up, not just the nausea. I do get the nausea as well, that wavy feeling in the stomach, but twice this week I vomited properly, in the morning, before I'd even had the tea. It's an awful start to the day.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has this morning pattern been going on?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Well I take the sumatriptan, the Imigran, when it hits. I thought they were the hundred milligram ones, but no, the box at home is the fifty, I checked it last night after Siobhan asked. I take one tablet by mouth, and if it's not gone I can take another after two hours, though I rarely do the second, and the chemist on Thomas Street said not to go over two in a day.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll come back to the tablets in a minute. What I was asking is how long the morning headaches and the vomiting have been happening.

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh right, sorry, I went off on one there. It's about three weeks, I think, could be four. It was after the long weekend, or maybe the week before that, I'm brutal with dates, and before that the migraines were the usual, one side, the light bothering me, maybe twice a month.

[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me play that back so I have it straight. Long-standing migraine, usually about twice a month, one-sided and light sensitive, and for roughly three to four weeks you've been waking with a bad headache, with nausea, and you've vomited twice this week. Is the new headache still on the one side?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly the left, same as always, behind the eye and into the temple. In the mornings though it feels more all over, like a tight band as well as the left side. The light still kills me, I have to keep the curtains shut, and the noise too, the radio is desperate even at a low volume.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or double vision with these?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. No funny speech, no double vision, no pins and needles, and I can move everything grand. I was worried it was a stroke because my uncle had one, but this doesn't feel like that to me.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): And between the headaches, during the day, are you yourself?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Once the tablet works I'm mostly grand for the rest of the day. My wife Siobhan says I snore the house down and that I'm tired all the time, wrecked, but I don't buy that at all. I'm not tired, I do a full day, I'm on my feet, I'm fine, and the snoring I wouldn't know because I'm asleep, but she goes on about it.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the headache actually wake you out of sleep, or is it there when the alarm goes?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): It's there when I wake. I don't think it wakes me, I sleep through until half six as far as I know. Then it's sitting there, and it's worse if I bend down to get the shoes, or if I cough, coughing makes it pound something fierce.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Coughing and bending making it worse is worth writing down. Any fever, or a stiff neck?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, I haven't felt hot or shivery. The neck's not stiff, I can look down at the phone grand. I had a cold about three weeks ago, just a runny nose for a few days, that's gone, and I wondered if that set this off but the cold is history.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you actually taking for the pain, day to day?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): The sumatriptan fifty milligrams, one tablet by mouth when the migraine is on me, and that's been two or three times a week the last month, which is more than my usual twice a month. Paracetamol on top of that, two of the five-hundred milligram tablets, I'd say three times a day most days for the last three weeks, sometimes four. I don't write it down, so I might be off by a dose.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any other tablets, blood pressure medicine, or, sorry, not the pill, you're not on that. Anything like ibuprofen from the chemist?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No blood pressure tablets, never been put on them. I did try ibuprofen last year for a sore back, the four-hundred milligram ones, but I stopped them because they tore the stomach, and I haven't taken one since, must be eight months. Just the sumatriptan and the paracetamol now, oh and a vitamin D from the supermarket, one a day, though that's hardly a medicine.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or to foods, or anything else?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing at all. I can take penicillin, I had it for a tooth years ago, no rash, no swelling, no problem. No food allergies either, I eat everything.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or take a drink?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I smoked in my twenties, about ten a day, and I gave them up when the first child was born, so that's twenty years off them. Drink is a few pints of a Saturday, two or three, and nothing through the week. I work in the warehouse at the hardware place on the industrial estate, lifting and that, so I'm fairly active, and we live out in Raheny, myself and Siobhan and the two teenagers.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): In the family, anyone with bad headaches, or tumours, or the stroke you mentioned?

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother gets migraines still, she's seventy-two and she manages them. My uncle Tom, that's my mother's brother, had a stroke at sixty-six, he's still with us but a bit weak on the one side. No tumours that I know of, and my dad had a stent in the heart a few years back, but that's him, not me, his heart is grand now he says.

[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. I'm not going to decide today that this is just the old migraine, or headaches from using the paracetamol and the extra sumatriptan, or something about your sleep because of what your wife says. Morning headache with vomiting, and pain worse when you cough, can be any of those, and it can also be a pressure problem we shouldn't shrug off. I won't conclude either way on the basis of the story alone.

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): A pressure problem, like a tumour? God. I've been googling that at two in the morning and Siobhan told me to cop on and stop, and I feel a bit sick even saying the word. I know Google is the worst doctor going.

[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not saying it is that. I'm saying I can't rule the worrying causes out from talking alone, and I'm not putting a label on it today. Let me examine you first and we'll go from there.

[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Look straight ahead for me. Your pupils are equal and they react to light, and there's no droop of the face. Squeeze my fingers, both hands are strong, and push up with the feet, that's strong too, and touch your nose with the finger, both sides, that's smooth. No stiff neck either, you can flex it fine.

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Did I pass? I was concentrating so hard I nearly forgot to breathe, which is ridiculous I know. The left hand might be a tiny bit weaker, I broke that finger years ago in a match, but you said both hands were strong so I'll take your word.

[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Both hands were strong, I wouldn't call the left weak. Walk to the door and back for me, thanks. Your gait is steady and you turn without any trouble, so that's a normal quick neurological exam.

[SEG0037] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry for sticking my head in, the next person is in the waiting room but you're grand for another few minutes. I left a urine bottle outside in case, though I don't think anyone asked for one. I'll get out of your way.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thanks, no urine sample needed, we're nearly done.

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. While you're writing, the vomiting was only those two mornings, not every day, and I don't want you thinking I'm puking constantly. Tuesday and this morning, that's the lot. The paracetamol I take with a glass of water, after food when I remember, if that matters at all.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Noted, two vomits this week, not daily. You were saying the sumatriptan is for when the migraine is on you. Does it actually clear the morning headache?

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): It takes the edge off after an hour or so, but the morning one doesn't clear the way the old ones did. I still have a dull ache until about lunchtime even after the tablet. Lying down in the dark helps a bit, and coffee sometimes helps the old migraine but it does nothing for this morning one, I tried that twice.

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the new morning headache is only partly helped by the sumatriptan, eases a little if you lie in the dark, and is worse with a cough or bending, while the older migraines still settle and coffee used to help those. Any change in your weight, or are you up at night passing water a lot?

[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Weight's the same, the belt's on the same hole, about eighty-two kilos, and it has been for years. I'm not up at night to the toilet, and the thirst is normal. I was going to tell you about the parking ticket I got outside, but that's not your problem, the warden was fierce.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Leaving the parking warden out of it. Any trouble with the vision apart from the light hurting, any blackouts, or any fits?

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): No blackouts, and no fits, I've never had a seizure in my life. The vision thing is just the light hurting, no black spots and no curtain coming down over the eye. I had the eyes tested in the spring and the optician said they were fine, but I don't have the letter on me.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm going to leave the scan for now rather than book it this morning. If the morning headache or the vomiting is no better in three weeks, or if you get a sudden worse headache, new weakness, or you're vomiting more, then we arrange a CT scan of the head. I'm not ordering it today.

[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks feels long if it's something bad, but if you think that's sound I'll go with it. Should I stop the paracetamol? I've read you can get headaches from taking too many painkillers, and I don't want to stop the sumatriptan, because that actually does something.

[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'd cut the paracetamol back rather than stop the sumatriptan. Use the paracetamol only when you need it, not three times every day, and keep the sumatriptan for the clear migraine attacks, one fifty-milligram tablet at the start, and no more than two days a week if you can. That's advice, I'm not changing the prescription today, and if you get more than two vomiting days in a week, ring us sooner.

[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, OK, two days a week for the sumatriptan, I'll try. The paracetamol is the harder one, because the dull ache just sits there. What if I take one five-hundred instead of two?

[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): One tablet won't do much for a headache like that. If you take it, take the two five-hundreds together, but not on a schedule. Come back and see me in three weeks anyway, whether or not we've gone for the scan, and reception can book that on your way out.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): If I vomit again over the weekend, do I wait, or do I come in? And can I drive? I drove here, it's about twenty minutes, and the light was bad but I managed it.

[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you vomit again and the headache is the same as today, you can wait for the three weeks, but if it's suddenly much worse, or you can't see properly, or you're confused, don't wait, go to the emergency department. Driving is fine if your vision is clear and you're not in the middle of an attack. I wouldn't drive during the bad morning pain.
[SEG0053] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book you in for three weeks with Dr O'Sullivan if you stop at the desk, and there's a leaflet on headache on the way out if you want it.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll take the leaflet. Thanks for not rushing me, I know I go on a bit. I'll mind the tablets and I'll be back in three weeks, please God.
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): You gave me a clear story, and that helps. Mind yourself, and you know the things that mean don't wait.

features: patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

bad.reason: All details supported except certainty; patient is not uncertain he has the symptom.
bad.text: Morning headache (category=neurological, status=present, severity=severe, duration=approximately 3 to 4 weeks, onset=present on waking, temporality=current, aggravating_factors=coughing; bending down, relieving_factors=sumatriptan, partial; lying in the dark, reported_by=patient, certainty=uncertain)

omissions.text: Morning headache is also described as more generalized in the mornings, 'all over' with a tight band sensation as well as left-sided behind the eye/temple.
Phonophobia/noise sensitivity was also part of the longstanding migraine symptoms ('the noise too, the radio is desperate even at a low volume').
Headache is present on waking but does not wake him from sleep; he sleeps through until about 6:30.
Vomiting occurred specifically on Tuesday and the morning of the visit, before tea, and not every day.

Sumatriptan dosing instructions from current use were more specific: one 50 mg tablet by mouth, may repeat after 2 hours, and he rarely takes the second tablet; pharmacist advised not more than two in a day.
Paracetamol route was oral as two 500 mg tablets, and he takes it most days for the last three weeks, sometimes four times daily.
He has not taken ibuprofen at all since it caused stomach upset, approximately eight months ago.
Allergy history was more specific: no medication or food allergies; he has tolerated penicillin previously without rash, swelling, or other problem.
Additional negative findings asked and answered are missing: no visual blackouts, no black spots, and no curtain coming down over the eye.

Doctor documented uncertainty/differential not captured: not deciding today whether this is old migraine, medication-overuse headache from paracetamol/extra sumatriptan, a sleep-related issue, or a raised-pressure problem; worrying causes cannot be ruled out from history alone.

The new morning headache is only partially relieved by sumatriptan and leaves a dull ache until about lunchtime; coffee does not help this new morning headache although it used to help the old migraines.
No brain tumour history in the family was specifically denied.
Recent relevant history: he had a cold with runny nose about three weeks ago that resolved, and he wondered if it triggered this.
He snores according to his wife, but he disputes being tired; possible sleep issue was raised by the doctor based on this history.
Plan nuance missing: the doctor explicitly said he was not ordering a CT scan today and was leaving the scan for now.
Safety-net advice omitted: if he has more than two vomiting days in a week, he should ring the clinic sooner.
Follow-up nuance missing: he was told to come back in three weeks anyway, whether or not a scan is arranged.
Driving advice was conditional: driving is fine if vision is clear and he is not in the middle of an attack, but he should not drive during the bad morning pain.
